extracted.intended_audience: readers and correspondents of Popular Science Monthly; general educated public interested in science, magazine editors and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial correspondence and commentary about standards for presenting scientific claims and handling advertising in a popular science magazine, plus a brief critique of superficial school science textbooks. Focuses on when it is appropriate to publish claims/ads and pedagogical approaches for public-school science.

rubrics_metrics.name: No use of remedies without known mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: If we do not know what a remedy is, and how it acts, we have no right, as honest men, to employ it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject 'rule-of-thumb' methods, charms, nostrums, and cures whose action is unknown. True medical practice should not rely on secret systems or mysterious remedies; the profession should not promote cures lacking explanatory/empirical basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting quackery and nostrums in professional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: There can not possibly be a 'system' or 'cure' in medicine. There are no rule-of-thumb methods, and no mysteries in true science... There is no system, or cure, or charm, or nostrum, known to the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public communication and professional practice should actively discourage belief in quackery. Editors and practitioners should avoid giving credibility to 'systems' that lack scientific grounding and should inform lay readers of the absence of such legitimate universal cures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising editorial boundary and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not think it would be easy to edit the advertisements... Meanwhile we agree not to sandwich advertisements through the text of the 'Monthly,' as is the custom with some journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policy: editors will not act as full fact-checkers for paid advertisements, but they should avoid embedding advertisements inside the main body/text (i.e., 'sandwiching' ads through articles). Complaints about dishonest ads should be directed to the magazine's advertising managers. The editors draw a practical boundary (here, 'we stop at the one hundred and forty-fourth page') to separate editorial content from advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of half-truths in advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst difficulty begins with those advertisements in which truth and falsehood are mixed; 'A lie that is half a truth is ever the blackest of lies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisements that blend truthful statements with misleading or false claims are especially harmful. As a normative criterion, such mixed-truth ads should be the focus of scrutiny and (where possible) corrective action by advertisers or advertising managers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical popularization of science
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim being ... popularizing it in the sense of giving the unprofessional reader the latest teachings of science without the rigorous processes of induction leading to such results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When popularizing science for a lay audience, present current scientific teachings but maintain skepticism about claims lacking rigorous backing. Avoid presenting unvetted cures or strong causal claims as settled fact; clarify when popular accounts omit the underlying rigorous evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial textbooks and rote recitation in school science
rubrics_metrics.description: We might have provided those boys and girls with copies of some one of the many text-books which profess to carry students over the entire subject in 'fourteen weeks,' or some other incredibly short time; we might have set those students to committing and reciting that text, but we didn't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on textbooks that promise to cover an entire discipline in an unrealistically short timeframe or reduce instruction to rote memorization and recitation. Prefer more substantive, extended, and non-rote pedagogical approaches for teaching 'natural philosophy' (science) in public schools.
